Ricollin Moodley: Lipstick Artist

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Some may use paint and brushes… but Ricollin Moodley uses nothing more than lipstick. Now the self-taught artist is gaining a large following from his unique art.

Unique Selling Point:
Ricollin Moodley: The Lipstick Artist
Ricollin Moodley, a self-taught artist from the South Coast of South Africa, has gained recognition for his unique art created using lipstick. His journey, filled with challenges, perseverance, and creativity, highlights his passion for art that helped him overcome adversity.
Early Life and Struggles
Born in Ladysmith, Ricollin grew up in a mixed-race family, with an Indian mother and a Xhosa father. Their marriage faced significant racial prejudice from both sides. For the first ten years, his parents lived apart due to these challenges. Financial hardship was a constant struggle, and his father’s income was barely enough to cover rent. During his teens, food was scarce, and Ricollin often took on the responsibility of finding meals for his family.
In 2017, Ricollin moved to Port Edward. As a Grade 11 student, he began exploring his passion for art, using discarded materials like library colouring pages to sketch. This creative outlet provided him a way to express his frustrations with his difficult circumstances.
The First Breakthrough
Ricollin’s first paying customer appeared while he was sketching on the beach, hungry after several days without food. A man approached and asked him to draw a portrait of his grandchild. In return, Ricollin asked for groceries. The man returned with not only groceries but also money and a phone (so he could start his journey as an artist). This act of kindness marked the beginning of Ricollin's career, showing him the potential of art as a means of survival.
The Rise of the Lipstick Artist
With the phone, Ricollin created a social media page to promote his work. Despite slow sales at first, he continued to take commissions and use art as a lifeline. In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic hit, and Ricollin’s father lost his job. The family became homeless for a while, but Ricollin began creating portraits in shopping malls, raising money for rent. The pressure of creating portraits quickly improved his skills.
Using Unconventional Mediums
Facing financial difficulties, Ricollin adapted by using whatever materials he could find. He used coffee grounds, food colouring, sand, and even discarded Woolworths shopping bags. His breakthrough came when he discovered a box of unused lipstick, which he began using as a medium. His "lipstick art" became a distinctive style, symbolising his journey of survival and transformation.


Summary:
Recognition and Growth
Ricollin’s work gained attention on social media, with celebrities like Tyla sharing his art, and even the Springboks following and commenting on his posts. In November 2023, he was invited by Siya Kolisi, captain of the Springboks, to attend a rugby match, where he had the chance to paint live at the event—an unforgettable experience for him and his family.
Though he hasn’t yet exhibited in galleries due to high fees, some galleries have bought his art at a low price and resold it for much more. Ricollin dreams of seeing his work displayed worldwide, believing that art can open doors and change lives.
A Life Transformed by Art
At 24, Ricollin Moodley’s story is one of resilience and passion. His journey proves that art is not only about skill but also about survival, hope, and vision. Despite facing significant challenges, Ricollin continues to build a future where his art connects with people globally, proving that creativity can truly transform lives.
Interviews:
We can visit Ricollin, as he lives in the South Coast near Margate. His parents are happy for us to interview them as well.
You may have seen him on the Supersport commercials about him drawing the team, after Siya and the guys made such a fuss of him on social media. He now has 129k followers! I’m sure Mnet/ Superport would love for us to celebrate him as well and highlight their ad with him.
Right now his family’s rent and income is solely based on his artwork, and we can go to his house and he’ll show us all his artworks, and we can watch him work – he’ll do a lipstick drawing of one of our presenters or of anyone of our choosing. He’s a really inspiring young man who is changing his life and that of his family’s by following his passion.




Further information:
Opening Sequence: The Mystery of Creation
Visuals:
The episode begins with a close-up of Ricollin’s hands moving across a canvas. The camera lingers on the movement of his fingers, the texture of the materials he’s using: lipstick, sand, coffee grounds. A match is lit, sand is sifted, and the cap of a lipstick is twisted off, all captured in slow motion, emphasizing the tactile nature of his creative process.
The shots are intimate and mysterious, hinting at the unconventional nature of his art without fully revealing it. There are tight shots of lipstick marks being made on paper, swipes of colour blending, creating something compelling but not yet clear.
VO: “As Ricollin’s work is beginning to reach audiences around the world, his journey as an artist goes far beyond the canvas. A life marked by hardship, resilience, and innovation has led him to this moment.”
The Big Reveal: Lipstick Art After a few moments of building suspense, the camera slowly zooms out to reveal the larger picture. Ricollin’s artwork takes shape—vibrant, expressive portraits or abstract figures created with the unique medium of lipstick. This reveal comes with a striking visual—a portrait that is hard to believe is made out of makeup.
The camera pulls back to reveal Ricollin at his easel, proudly standing before his creation. The artistry becomes clear. We see him as the artist who works with lipstick, turning a product associated with beauty into a powerful medium for personal expression.
Sound:
The sound design is minimalist, with each action punctuated by the subtle scratch of lipstick on canvas, the gentle sifting of sand, and a soft, atmospheric musical score. The visuals and sound build suspense, creating a sense of wonder about what he is creating. When we reveal the painting, the music swells, signifying the moment of revelation. There is a slight shift in tone from mystery to awe, celebrating Ricollin's innovative approach to art.
ACT 1:
Transition to Interview: The Artist’s Story
Visuals:
We transition to a more relaxed setting, where Ricollin is seated at his home in the South Coast, ready for an in-depth interview. The camera frames him thoughtfully, showing the warmth of his personality. This moment is grounded, and the visuals switch from the intensity of creation to a more reflective tone.
Interview with Ricollin Moodley: Themes of Family and Struggle
Visuals:
The interview unfolds with Ricollin sharing his backstory. As he speaks, we will use Broll with his parents, photos from his childhood, and images of his early sketches. We see Ricollin’s family life, the challenges his parents faced with racial prejudice, their financial struggles, and the toll it took on his mother’s health.
Narrative Arcs:
• Growing up in a mixed-race family: One point of tension is when Ricollin talks about his parents' marriage and the prejudices they faced—his Indian mother, Evelyn Moodley, and his Xhosa father, Sivuyile Masola. He describes the impact of these challenges on his childhood and how their love endured despite the pressures.
• Financial hardship and responsibility: Another point of tension is where Ricollin shares the difficulties his family faced, from financial hardship to food scarcity. He recounts how, as a teenager, he often took on the responsibility of providing for his family, finding food during difficult times. His response to this tension for to create art to support his family. Ricollin recounts the pivotal moment when a stranger approached him while he was sketching on the beach, offering him a commission in exchange for food. This simple act of kindness, which included not just groceries but a phone, was the turning point in Ricollin’s life, marking the beginning of his career as an artist.
In this first act we are going to see Ricollin begin making an artwork… but we will only reveal this at the end of the program. In order for him to do this, we need to decide now what he must do as we need to get him the correct tools. If we want a lipstick portrait he will need the right canvas and lipsticks, SuperSport gave a few thousand to assist with costs of this, so we just need to figure what we can budget. A simple sketch portrait is quick, but not as detailed as I think we are hoping. I’ll put costs for this below – and we can discuss. But we will show the visuals of this being built throughout the piece. For now this will be a portrait of Claire the presenter…
ACT 2:
The Unconventional Medium: Lipstick and Survival
Visuals:
We move to a sequence where Ricollin explains how he adapted his artistry in response to financial difficulty. We see shots of him using unconventional materials like coffee grounds, food colouring, sand, and even discarded Woolworths shopping bags. The camera zooms in on Ricollin’s hands as he applies lipstick to the canvas—his distinctive medium for creation.
Ricollin explains how he came across a box of unused lipstick and how that marked the beginning of his unique style. The camera focuses on the layers of lipstick on the canvas, creating intricate textures and rich, emotional visuals.
Interview Highlight:
• Ricollin’s take on using lipstick: “It became more than just a material—it was a symbol of transformation. My art has always been about survival and renewal.”
We will also have introduced his parents Evelyn and Sivuyile. Sivu works at Spar currently and has different shifts, so we can maybe show him returning home and see his wife who is sick and can’t take care of herself. They’ll talk about his artwork and just what a difference this has made in their lives.
Continuing visually to show him creating painting of Claire:
There needs to be a change of pace here in the story: A shot of Ricollin’s face, intent, concentrated, and absorbed in his process, slowly transitions to a slightly wider shot—his workspace beginning to take shape in the background. We see his tools: creating a sense of intrigue and curiosity. The cuts are quick, sharp—each shot adding to the mystery. We see something obscure: a figure but we never quite see it fully. The audience is left questioning what he’s making—what the materials mean, what the process is building toward.
ACT 3:
The Transformation: A Life Built Through Art Visuals:
We cut to a more recent shot of Ricollin, now becoming quite successful on social media, actively engaging with his growing online community. His Instagram feed https://www.instagram.com/ricollinart_official/reels/?hl=en
shows his diverse artwork and growing following to 129k. We see Ricollin’s efforts to mentor others, offering tutorials on how to use lipstick as an artistic medium and inspiring others to pursue their creative passions.
VO: “From struggling to make ends meet to becoming an artist who not only creates but helps others unlock their own potential, Ricollin’s story is one of transformation and hope. Through art, he has found a way to not just survive, but thrive.”
The Future: A New Path Forward Visuals:
The final moments of the program show Ricollin at work in his studio, reflecting on how far he’s come and where he wants to go. His artwork is being signed by the Springboks and how he had such a great experience with Siya Kolisi and his influence is spreading globally.
We can talk about his DSTV young creator nomination and the work he’s done with Supersport since Siya Kolisi and some of the boks shared his art work. I’ve asked Supersport for some of those visuals.
Interview Highlight:
• Ricollin on his future: “Art is always evolving, just like life. I’m excited for what’s ahead—for the art, for the people I can inspire, and for the stories still to be told.”
Sound:
The music swells into a hopeful, inspiring theme, signifying the possibilities of the future. The camera slowly fades out from Ricollin’s studio to a final image of him standing confidently in front of his work.
Closing: Legacy of Hope
Visuals:
We end with a final shot of one of Ricollin’s piece he’s been creating while we were filming him…This for now is Claire’s portait…
VO: We often look for answers in art. But sometimes, the journey of creating is the answer itself. Ricollin Moodley doesn’t just create; he transforms the ordinary into the extraordinary, bringing together materials that seem disparate, yet together tell a story only he can express.”
Ricollin: “Art is the conversation between the material and the emotion. It’s not about what you see, but what you feel.”
Timing:
Ricolling is away next week for an event, and so we would need to shoot this sooner, he asked if we can maybe even be there on a Saturday morning as his father works shifts at spar…
COSTS:
Claire the presenter, myself and the cameraman would fly down to Margate. It’s 30 mins from Shelly Beach South Coast KZN.

Portaits come in stages…tension…
Photo…location – drawing in garage and intv different…


IDEAS:
Time-lapse of the Painting Process
• Idea: Set up a stationary camera to capture the entire painting from start to finish in a time-lapse format. This gives viewers a sense of the artist’s process and how the painting evolves.
• Creative Twist: Integrate several angles of the canvas over time. Start with a wide shot and gradually zoom in as the painting becomes more detailed.
Close-up Shots of Tools & Materials
• Idea: Focus on the liptsticks and the materials being used, as well as the process, the brushstrokes, capture that shot of what it looks like from the Canvas’ point of view, so you see his face as he’s painting. Capture the texture of the lipstick and the motion of his hand – which actually a very unusual position.
• Use macro shots or slow mo shots for stunning detail shots
An idea? We can take Ricollin outside and film him painting at the beach. Capture the environment around them, have all the environmental sounds, such as wind, birds, or traffic, to evoke a specific atmosphere that enhances the visual storytelling.
Another Idea? Film the painting process backwards, starting with the completed artwork and moving to the blank canvas. This can be an intriguing visual representation of creativity. We could also use slow motion or reverse time-lapse to add drama to the action of "undoing" the work.

Another idea: Split-Screen/Multiview?
Use a split-screen effect to show multiple angles at the same time—such as a top-down view of the canvas, a profile shot of the artist’s face, and close-ups of the painting’s details. Include elements like the artist walking around the canvas or moving their body in ways that pull the viewer into the experience. Highlight contrasting elements like the calm, meditative process of painting versus the intensity of the artist’s facial expressions or body movements.




Extra Budget Items:
We would need to rent a car and have 1 night stay over in order to get everything.
We also need to supply art supplies for him to create a painting/drawing…
I asked Ricollin what he sent supersport in terms of his supply needs:
Canvas R1200
Lipsticks (about 20 lipsticks) R1700 Shades he needs are blacks, yellows, blues and skin tone shades
Sealant to seal the painting will be R800
Makeup sponges to use for the painting R100
The total amount is R3800
If this is too much, we can discuss it and see how we can bring it down.
Riccolin keeps his artwork afterwards, so as we wont pay him for the time etc I think that's reasonable.


Suggested shot list:
Walk on beach – wind in his hair, that feeling of freedom, sketching on the beach
Family eating a meal together or interacting in the home
Walking around the area his home area, and checking the bins for useful trash that he can make art out of

We would interview him in a gallery and have him looking at modern art.
I see Supersport did a recreation of the German man on the beach incident so we can use that as I’ve secured their footage.
There are some videos of him at the mall etc

Ric: so I literally knew nothing about art but I had this passion and at that moment the desperation to find a way to get food allowed that talent to be you know come out

Ric: There was no words to describe his reaction. He went and he came back with groceries, a phone and an envelope that had money in it and he told me that I must never underestimate my value.

Ric: I started painting with coffee, food coloring, sand, leaves whatever around me that I could use, I even created clothes with reusable shopping bags.
Show video from instagram of him with shopping bags…See the johnny depp coffee video
Claire: It’s actually made from coffee, that blew my mind.

Ric: I was already you know passionate about creating unique art so it's just I went looking and then I came across the box of thrown away lipsticks and makeup
that's literally the first time I created uh my lipstick paintings. When I started I took whatever brands I could find I took whatever colors I could find.
VO 16: It’s become his signature medium.
VO 17: But with it came challenges.
Ric: They smudge um they when in the sun they melt, they fade. so I spent a lot of time trying to find a way to seal these paintings and eventually I came up with my own combination that's like my secret.

(WE WILL HAVE TO COVER THIS COMMENT COS SHE DOESN’T SAY IT RIGHT THERE)

Ric: like the galleries
they said that I need to pay this amount, my work is not good enough some galleries did buy my works for 50 rand hundred rand and then I found out that they were selling it for 10,000, 20 thousand rand.
VO 19: Despite it all, Ricollin says, when he’s creating, his mind is quiet.
Ric: I wanna find things that's more challenging, out of the box, create conversations, art is not limited to just a paint and brush.

Ric: My parents for the first 10 years of their marriage they've been apart because of the family is not wanting each other my mom's family not wanting my dad's family because of the the the race

Evelyn: so we said to each other you're only pointing out the differences but you're not pointing out the fact that Evelyn and me can't live without each another. We didn't choose to be different nations but we love each another and we created this family.

As he speaks, we will use Broll with his parents, photos from his childhood, and images of his early sketches. We see Ricollin’s family life, the challenges his parents faced with racial prejudice, their financial struggles, and the toll it took on his mother’s health. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Some may use paint and brushes… but Ricollin Moodley uses nothing more than lipstick. Now the self-taught artist is gaining a large following from his unique art.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Ricollin Moodley: The Lipstick Artist Ricollin Moodley, a self-taught artist from the South Coast of South Africa, has gained recognition for his unique art created using lipstick. His journey, filled with challenges, perseverance, and creativity, highlights his passion for art that helped him overcome adversity. Early Life and Struggles Born in Ladysmith, Ricollin grew up in a mixed-race family, with an Indian mother and a Xhosa father. Their marriage faced significant racial prejudice from both sides. For the first ten years, his parents lived apart due to these challenges. Financial hardship was a constant struggle, and his father’s income was barely enough to cover rent. During his teens, food was scarce, and Ricollin often took on the responsibility of finding meals for his family. In 2017, Ricollin moved to Port Edward. As a Grade 11 student, he began exploring his passion for art, using discarded materials like library colouring pages to sketch. This creative outlet provided him a way to express his frustrations with his difficult circumstances. The First Breakthrough Ricollin’s first paying customer appeared while he was sketching on the beach, hungry after several days without food. A man approached and asked him to draw a portrait of his grandchild. In return, Ricollin asked for groceries. The man returned with not only groceries but also money and a phone (so he could start his journey as an artist). This act of kindness marked the beginning of Ricollin's career, showing him the potential of art as a means of survival. The Rise of the Lipstick Artist With the phone, Ricollin created a social media page to promote his work. Despite slow sales at first, he continued to take commissions and use art as a lifeline. In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic hit, and Ricollin’s father lost his job. The family became homeless for a while, but Ricollin began creating portraits in shopping malls, raising money for rent. The pressure of creating portraits quickly improved his skills. Using Unconventional Mediums Facing financial difficulties, Ricollin adapted by using whatever materials he could find. He used coffee grounds, food colouring, sand, and even discarded Woolworths shopping bags. His breakthrough came when he discovered a box of unused lipstick, which he began using as a medium. His "lipstick art" became a distinctive style, symbolising his journey of survival and transformation.
metadata.Summary: Recognition and Growth Ricollin’s work gained attention on social media, with celebrities like Tyla sharing his art, and even the Springboks following and commenting on his posts. In November 2023, he was invited by Siya Kolisi, captain of the Springboks, to attend a rugby match, where he had the chance to paint live at the event—an unforgettable experience for him and his family. Though he hasn’t yet exhibited in galleries due to high fees, some galleries have bought his art at a low price and resold it for much more. Ricollin dreams of seeing his work displayed worldwide, believing that art can open doors and change lives. A Life Transformed by Art At 24, Ricollin Moodley’s story is one of resilience and passion. His journey proves that art is not only about skill but also about survival, hope, and vision. Despite facing significant challenges, Ricollin continues to build a future where his art connects with people globally, proving that creativity can truly transform lives. Interviews: We can visit Ricollin, as he lives in the South Coast near Margate. His parents are happy for us to interview them as well. You may have seen him on the Supersport commercials about him drawing the team, after Siya and the guys made such a fuss of him on social media. He now has 129k followers! I’m sure Mnet/ Superport would love for us to celebrate him as well and highlight their ad with him. Right now his family’s rent and income is solely based on his artwork, and we can go to his house and he’ll show us all his artworks, and we can watch him work – he’ll do a lipstick drawing of one of our presenters or of anyone of our choosing. He’s a really inspiring young man who is changing his life and that of his family’s by following his passion.

Film the painting process backwards, starting with the completed artwork and moving to the blank canvas. This can be an intriguing visual representation of creativity. We could also use slow motion or reverse time-lapse to add drama to the action of "undoing" the work. Another idea: Split-Screen/Multiview? Use a split-screen effect to show multiple angles at the same time—such as a top-down view of the canvas, a profile shot of the artist’s face, and close-ups of the painting’s details. Include elements like the artist walking around the canvas or moving their body in ways that pull the viewer into the experience. Highlight contrasting elements like the calm, meditative process of painting versus the intensity of the artist’s facial expressions or body movements.
